items.title: What the Postcards Left Out: Hauptstraße in Pustchow
items.summary: Every postcard is an advertisement. Someone chooses the spot, the season and the caption, framing a single view for visitors…
items.content_html:
Every postcard is an advertisement. Someone chooses the spot, the season and the caption, framing a single view for visitors to send home. A camera, however, takes in more than its owner intends. At the edges of the frame, in the ruts of a road, the line of a fence or a small sign nobody was meant to read, the picture keeps what the advertisement leaves out. Read slowly, detail by detail, and a simple postcard becomes evidence.

Take today's Słoneczna Street in Pustkowo. Until 1945 the village was known as Pustchow, and the street was simply called Hauptstraße, the main street. Three postcards from the 1920s and 1930s show it from opposite ends. Set side by side, the three images reveal what no caption mentions: a farming village slowly turning into a resort, and a state moving quietly into the most ordinary of places.

From Farm Lane to Idyll, 1925 and 1933

The earliest photograph, taken around 1925 from today's corner of Spacerowa, looks east and shows Hauptstraße stretching empty under a heavy sky. There is no paving, only loose sand cut by deep ruts where cart wheels kept falling into the same tracks. On either side of the road rises a gabled house.

That sand is not a sign of neglect, but the result of Prussian road law. Provinces and districts had the funds and engineers to provide paving, while local streets were left to the community itself. Laying cobbles meant raising money that a small settlement could rarely spare. Not surprisingly, well into the 1930s, a number of Pomeranian villages still lacked a single paved road. Hauptstraße was the spine of Pustchow, yet underfoot it remained a country lane.

If the sand belonged to the village, the birches belonged to the state. Along the left edge especially, they stand too evenly spaced to have seeded themselves. Lining roads with trees was an old Prussian practice: from the late eighteenth century, the state planted its new roads by decree, and district offices kept nurseries to supply village streets. Birch suited Pustchow because it thrives on dry, poor sand where other trees struggle.

When, around 1933, a photographer returned to the same spot, almost nothing on the street had changed. The sand looks firmer, levelled perhaps, or simply flattened by the summer light, yet there are still no cobbles or kerbs. Where the earlier postcard feels raw and damp, this one is tranquil, with the birches and houses standing undisturbed. Both cards carry the label Ostseebad Pustchow, Baltic seaside resort. No authority granted that title: before the First World War, 142 places on the German Baltic coast called themselves Ostseebad, all competing for visitors from the cities. Yet on closer inspection, something has changed after all: the way the village was presented.

While the older postcard captions the scene with the plain street name, the one from 1933 drops Hauptstraße altogether for something far more evocative: Dorf-Idyll, village idyll. Three figures in smart clothes stroll down the unpaved lane towards the camera. Who are they? Guesthouse owners, villagers, or perhaps the guests themselves. What matters is how they come across: as if embodying a new idea of the countryside, unhurried, unspoiled, made for leisure. Nobody in the picture is working. A small resort could not sell grand promenades, so it sold an idyll instead.

Out of Season, 1938

A third postcard reverses the view. Its photographer stood at the far end of Hauptstraße, at today's corner of Magdaleny, and looked back west, bringing two other houses and a boarded fence into the frame. Some five years after the Dorf-Idyll card, the mood feels harsher.

At first, the change seems only seasonal. The trees are almost bare, so the picture was taken outside the summer months. On the right lies the garden of Zimdars' Gesellschaftshaus, an inn and meeting hall where villagers and holidaymakers sat at the same tables. On this day every bench is empty: the visitors have not yet come, or have already left.

Beyond the garden, a long fence of closed vertical boards runs towards Haus Kiese, the guesthouse visible further down the street. Solid boards do more than mark a boundary: they keep out the wind, the blowing sand and the eyes of passers-by. They belong to a street that now had guests, and to the privacy guests expected.

The quiet of the empty garden, however, hides a deeper change. Beside the building stand two tall, bare poles. From 1935, the swastika was Germany's only national flag, and on every official holiday it would have flown above the inn.

A Sign at the Edge of the Village

Across the road, at the left edge of the postcard, is the detail easiest to overlook, and yet the most precise: a small sign. Four lines of lettering read:

Pustchow

(Zollgrenzbezirk)

Kreis Greifenberg

Reg.-Bez. Stettin

Pustchow

(Customs-Border District)

Greifenberg District

Stettin Administrative Region

The wording fixes the date. Starting in January 1938, traffic rules required signs in border districts to carry this designation. The last two lines place the Greifenberg district (today Gryfice) within the Stettin (Szczecin) administration, a status that ended that October, when it was transferred to Köslin (Koszalin). While signs were not always replaced overnight, this one fits the months in between, and the bare trees narrow the moment to the spring of 1938.

For Pustchow, that boundary was the sea, just north of the village, behind the cliff. A year earlier, Germany's customs patrol had been reorganised as the Zollgrenzschutz (border guard). The force recruited mainly former soldiers, supported by SA and SS auxiliaries. No uniform appears on the card, yet the state stands at the entrance to the village, in a four-line inscription.

One Street, Three Histories

Together, the three cards show one short street carrying three histories at once. The sand and the ruts belong to the farming village. The caption Dorf-Idyll, the garden and the closed fence belong to the resort trade, which was turning a working street into a view. The birches, the poles and the sign belong to the state, which planted the trees, raised the flags and turned the sea into a guarded border. In the spring of 1938, a year and a half before the war, all three threads met on Hauptstraße, under bare branches, beside an empty garden.

The sand, the birches and the board fence have since gone. So have the Zimdars inn and Haus Kiese, the sign and the poles. Only the two gabled houses from the western view still stand; the one on the right also appears in the guide's first chapter. The postcards were made to sell an idyll. Read at their edges, they keep everything the idyll left out.
